questions.prompt: What is the difference between an outcome label and a label of what should have happened?
options: An outcome label is a probability, and a 'should have happened' label is a category
An outcome label records what actually happened - read out of the ticket queue, the CRM or the logs - while a 'should have happened' label records one person's reading of the case
An outcome label is written by a machine, and a 'should have happened' label is written by a human
There is no difference; they are two names for the same thing
questions.explain: Outcome labels are read from the record of the work: which team handled the ticket, how it was closed, whether the customer churned. That is what makes them trustworthy, and it is why they can be bootstrapped cheaply. A 'should have happened' label is one person's judgement, and the person writing it is not the population the model serves - so when the model disagrees you cannot tell who is wrong. Probability versus category is the noul/choice distinction, not this one. Machine versus human is not the dividing line either - a human writes outcome labels all the time when reading them out of a queue.

questions.prompt: Your model scores 88% on a battery whose two labellers agreed on only 90% of the cases. What does that tell you about the 88%?
options: That the labellers were careless and the 88% should be trusted
That the model is 2% worse than the labellers, which is a meaningful gap
That the model should be re-run with more repeats
That the benchmark has roughly a 10% floor of inherent disagreement built into it, so the 88% carries substantial uncertainty and the model may be within noise of the labellers themselves
questions.explain: If two careful labellers disagree on about 10% of cases, then the labels themselves contain roughly 10% of irreducible uncertainty. A reported 88% therefore has to be read with that error bar: the model may be indistinguishable from the labellers, and '88% vs 90%' is not a finding. Option 2 mistakes disagreement for carelessness - genuine ambiguity is the usual cause. Option 3 compares a number against a number measured on different cases. Option 4 confuses two different sources of noise: repeats test the model's stability, not the label's.

questions.prompt: Two labellers disagree on a borderline ticket. What should adjudication do?
options: Take the majority view of whoever is most senior, and discard the disagreement
Average the two labels into a half-way value
Drop the case from the battery, since it cannot be labelled reliably
Resolve it to the label the work actually justified - and record the disagreement, because it marks the case as ambiguous and belongs in a separate borderline slice of the results
questions.explain: Adjudication is a process, not a vote: the adjudicator picks the label the actual work justified - often by going back to what the team that handled it really did - and the disagreement is kept, not erased, because it tells you where the task is ambiguous and where the model's competence is actually visible. Seniority is a tie-break at best, and erasing the disagreement destroys the information. Averaging is meaningless: a gold label is a categorical answer, not a number. Dropping the case quietly biases the benchmark toward easy cases and inflates every headline number.

questions.prompt: Why can a wrong gold label make a good model look bad - and what is the opposite error?
options: A wrong label raises accuracy artificially; the opposite error lowers it artificially
A wrong label changes the cost of the run; the opposite error changes the latency
There is no opposite error - a wrong label is only ever harmful in one direction
A wrong label marks a correct answer as wrong; the opposite error rewards the wrong behaviour and makes a bad model look good, which is worse because the benchmark now teaches the mistake
questions.explain: Labels are the target, so the metric rewards whatever they say. If your label says 'sales' and the truth was 'billing', a model that routes correctly to billing is marked wrong - the bad direction. The opposite - a label that says 'billing' when the truth was 'sales' - makes a model that routes to sales look right, and the benchmark then actively rewards the mistake. That second error is more dangerous because it is invisible: the accuracy goes up and nothing looks wrong. Cost and latency are unaffected by labels.

questions.prompt: Connect this to the repo: why can cases/injection.json and cases/format_variants.json have no gold labels at all, while cases/routing.json needs them?
options: Because the injection and format batteries are too small to label
Because the mock provider cannot read gold labels

Because the routing battery is scored by comparing the model's answers against a right answer (accuracy, Brier, ECE all need an outcome), while the injection and format batteries are scored by how much the answer CHANGES - which needs no right answer at all
Because gold labels are only permitted in the routing battery for licensing reasons
questions.explain: run_battery() only calls metrics.score_case() when the case has a gold entry, and score_case() is what produces accuracy, Brier and ECE - every one of those needs an outcome to compare against. The injection battery measures whether the decision flipped (action_change_rate against thresholds) and the format battery measures how far the probability moved (spread and flips_at_0.5). Neither has a right answer to compare with, so neither needs a label. That contrast is exactly why the format-friction experiment was the cheapest one in the field. The other three options are wrong: there is no licensing rule, the batteries are the same size, and the mock never sees a gold label - it produces answers only.
